title: Hacker's Guide to Deep Learning

sentences.text: Today we're going to have a lecture which is a little bit different than some of the other ones because it's a bit more on just practical advice and heuristics and hacks, a little less on formal knowledge and theory.
So the big disclaimer is that this is going to be a somewhat opinionated lecture.
I'll share things that I think are good ideas, but they're not what everybody would agree on.
It's just anecdotes from my own experience.

And we'll talk about a bunch of different aspects of the deep learning pipeline and how to actually make working systems with data and models and good optimizers, and also then some comments on the other parts of the problem, like how do you create a good evaluation framework and how do you use compute effectively and so forth.
And these slides are put together from a lot of sources.
So in particular, Evan Shelhamer had a talk which formed the skeleton of this talk that he was giving for some years.
Evan was the developer of Caffe, which was the most popular deep learning framework 5 or 10 years ago.
And then I got a lot of tips from Andrej Karpathy's blog posts on this topic and from my lab members and other folks.
OK.
So the starting point of this lecture is that a big part of the story of deep learning is not just the theory or the algorithms, it's actually the hacks, the practical tips.
It's a little bit of a triumph of the practitioners over the academics and the theorists.
It doesn't mean that we won't eventually have a very clean mathematical theory of deep learning.
But historically, a lot of the people that have really made progress here have just done these things which we might call hacking.
And it's worth valuing that and understanding that.
And in the generalization lecture, I talked about this paper briefly, which is that you can overfit to a set of random labels with a deep net.
And this means that the generalization bounds you get from some classical theories, like the VC dimension, are vacuous.
They don't really tell you anything about how well that system will generalize.
And yet, deep nets generalize.
So clearly, the classical theory doesn't quite work.

And a lot of the places you may have been introduced to deep learning, if you've studied it in the past or you've programmed with neural nets in the past, would be courses that are very practical in nature, like fast.ai, which are really focused on, let's just code these systems and make them run,
and maybe the math and the theory is secondary.
OK.
So this practical stuff is a big part of the story, and it's worth understanding.
So I'm going to start with one story, which comes from my postdoc advisor, Alyosha Efros, here on the right, back when I was at Berkeley.
And his advisor, Jitendra Malik, on the left, was mentoring Alyosha when Alyosha was a grad student.
So this has been passed down to me through multiple generations.
And essentially, Alyosha was training models back in those days, 10, 20 years ago and would come to Jitendra, his advisor, and say, OK, here is my result. And it wasn't a deep net.
It was something else.
But this is just meant to convey the idea that he would show the results of some numbers, some plot, like, oh, I got 30% accuracy.
Or maybe here's my loss or my optimization graph.
And Jitendra would say, OK, what's going on here?
Why are these spikes?
And Alyosha would say, well, I don't know.
And so Jitendra said, OK, this is not enough.
This doesn't tell you that much about what's going on.
You really have to look at the data.
You have to look at the results that you're getting.
This was a computer vision lab.
And so the data was images.
Look at the images.
Look at what images you're analyzing, what labels you're predicting.
Look at the data.
Don't just give me some summary statistic.
And he put it this way.
He said, "Become friends with every pixel."
So I think that's just a lovely phrase.
And whatever domain you're in, try to become friends with the data points in that domain.
If you're studying music, become friends with every note.
If you're studying chemistry, become friends with every molecule.
Become friends with every pixel.
Look at the data.
OK.
So then Alyosha is well known in computer vision now as being a very intuitive and insightful person, in terms of the holistic nature of computer vision.
He went to France and took photos and understood the beauty of that data type.
OK.
So look at the data.
And you can think about this also for your final projects.
Don't just show us a plot.
Show us the data, something a little bit more high dimensional than just a single plot.
Here's an example from a system that tried to diagnose whether or not a scan of a patient's chest-- this patient has breast cancer or not.
And so you're trying to classify benign or malignant for the possibility of there being a tumor.
And this paper is actually an analysis and critique of prior work.
So it's not their fault. These authors were the ones that pointed out this issue.
But what happened is, a deep net was used in prior work to try to identify, is this cancerous or not?
And it got really high accuracy-- I don't know-- 99% accuracy.
So what do you think it was doing.
Anyone maybe have seen cases like this?
Was this deep net accurately classifying the scan?
Actually, I'll tell you.
I'll tell you, it wasn't.
So they then tested this system, and it failed.
So why did it fail?
What was it doing that made it fail?
I saw an answer back here.
So nothing is cancerous.
Yeah.
So one answer-- it just said nothing is cancerous.
And maybe the data set is imbalanced, so 99% of the cases were not cancerous.
That could have been it.
That's not the case in this one, but that is a common failure.
Let's go back here.
It was looking at stuff outside of the lungs.
Like, maybe the R in the top right corner is more often seen in cancers.
That was the point they were trying to make.
So in this case, as you said, the deep net was not looking at the tissue.
It was looking at the R in the corner.
So there was this kind of spurious correlation, this shortcut.
And it turned out that that R was some indicator about what hospital this came from or-- I don't remember entirely.
But let's just imagine that it was R if it came from Roosevelt Hospital or something like that.
And at Roosevelt Hospital, all the patients that were put into the system had malignant tumors because it was a hospital you go to for that situation.
So there was a bias in the data, and the data gave away the answer.
And so you really need to look at these things to identify, is your model working for the right reason or the wrong reason?
This is the wrong reason because it won't generalize to other hospitals.
OK.
Or you can imagine a worst case, where R just meant malignant, and it would have a different symbol if it weren't.
It would just completely give away the answer, and it wouldn't generalize to a system that doesn't give you the answer.
And that's what you really care about.
OK.
Look at the output too.
So don't just look at your loss curve.
That's the most superficial thing.
You should definitely do that, but don't only do that.
So here is something that would be better to look at if you're in the business of training generative models of cats.
We'll talk about generative models later.
But these are models that make photos of-- you've all seen this, DALL-E and Midjourney and these types of things.
So this is learning to make photos of cats.
And if I were to only look at my loss, like, what does my objective function say about the quality of these images?
It might be spiky and crazy.
I don't know what's going on.
But if I look at samples from the model-- actually, these are outputs from the model as it's being trained-- you get a lot more information.
You can kind of see something, which is like, it seems to oscillate.
It's, like, periodic.
So now this happens to be what's called a generative adversarial network.
We'll talk a little bit about these later.
But they do have this oscillatory behavior.
And it's something that's very obvious in this output.
It would also maybe be obvious in certain loss curves.
But you get a much higher-dimensional, high-throughput understanding of what's going on when you actually look at the data like this.
OK.
Oh, here's another example.
These are some little ants that I trained years ago to try to play some predator-prey game.
And what was happening is they would-- I looked at the reward function.
This is like a reinforcement learning.
They're trying to chase each other.
I think that the blue ones are trying to run away from the red ones, which are the predators.
And at first, the reward of the predators would go up a little bit, but then it would just plateau.
And I didn't know what was going on.
And why was it plateauing?
Because they were falling over and then making no more progress.
So if I only looked at the loss, it was like, oh, it just plateaued.
Learning is hard.
I don't know.
SGD was failing.
No, it was failing for a very particular reason, which is that the ants fell over and I had to fix that.
OK.
So look at your outputs.
Look at your inputs.
Visualize what you're doing.
OK.
So just to summarize some of those points-- look at the data.
Inspect the distribution of inputs in your training set.
Inspect the distribution of outputs in your training set.
As the student said over here, you could have an imbalanced set of target outputs in your training data, and that would be another common failure.

If your data is 99% benign tumors and 1% malignant, then chance, where the system is completely doing naive guessing based on those priors, not looking at the data, not looking at the input at all would be 99%.
You could just say, well, I know I'll be 99% right if I always say benign.
Then you have to calibrate with respect to that.
You have to realize that 99% is trivial.
And therefore, you're looking for a higher number than this.
Or maybe you want to measure something else, like the conditional probability of being correct, given that it's malignant.
OK.
So you can select random mini batches.
You can visualize them, plot histograms, plot marginal statistics.
What is the variability of the units of measure in your data?
Are your numbers in the range 0 to 1, or in the range 0 to 256, or in some other range?
Can negative numbers be your data, or is it only positive numbers?
These are the types of things you want to know.
OK.
So one of the most common bugs that I come across, especially in final projects, is that the data is not being preprocessed and loaded into the format that you think it is.
So, for example, let's say you're working with images, and you have assumed that your data lies in the range 0 to 1.
But actually, when you loaded it, it is loaded as a unsigned integer 8, uint8's in the range 0 to 255, which is a common format for imagery.
So you might have a bug because you have code that-- let's say you actually clamp your inputs to be between 0 and 1, but the data you're loading is between 0 and 255.
So now you're losing all of the information because you're making all your data points equal to either 0 or 1.
So you have to be very careful about this.
And what I would recommend-- and I think it's just a very simple recipe-- is, somewhere in your code, you're going to have model.forward, right?
You're going to run your neural net in a forward pass on your data point.
Right before that line is where you should inspect the data.
So you don't want to inspect the data as it's sorting your hard drive.
You don't want to inspect the data as it's initially loaded by your data loader.
You can do that too, but the place where you really need to understand what the format of the data is and what the distribution of the data is right before you run your model on it.
And make sure that what format you think it is, what shape you think it has, what dimensionality you think it has, exactly matches what it actually is in practice.
OK.
So here's just another example of where this can go wrong.
So it turns out that in some of these old neural net libraries-- one is called DeCAF.
Another is called Caffe.
So these are like the precursors of PyTorch and TensorFlow and other models like that, other systems like that.
If you load an image off of your desk, in DeCAF, it will be represented upside down.
It'll be flipped.
And in Caffe, the channels will be permuted.
So the standard color space for Caffe is BGR instead of RGB.
The color channels are permuted.
And so if I have an image on disk and it's in RGB order and then I load it into Caffe, the order of the channels will be-- the blue channel is in the first channel dimension, the first index.
So that was because of some old convention in a library called OpenCV.
It doesn't really matter, but it used to be BGR was the convention, and now we use RGB as a convention.
But let's say that I'm training my Caffe model on images.
And maybe it says-- oh, this is a blueberry, right?

Well, that could be because it's actually seen an object which has a strong red channel, but it's interpreting that red channel as the color blue because maybe the system was pre-trained on data in the format RGB.
But now you load it into Caffe, and it's in the framework BGR.
So anyway, you can get errors like this.
So you really need to have a match between what your model is expecting and what you're giving it.
And if there's any mismatch between training and inference, or between the model architecture and the numerical transformations you apply and the data format, then this will cause problems.
OK.
So here's, I think, the most important function in deep learning.
This is one that I wrote.
So it's a very clever advanced contribution.
OK.
So here it is.
Inspect data.
OK.
So I just put this all over in code that I write.
Right before you called model.forward, that's the most important place to put this.
But you can just sprinkle it all throughout your code.
OK.
It's going to just tell you a few things.
And to me, these are the most important things to know about your data, but there's a lot more you could think of as well.
Again, you could try to visualize it somehow or plot two-dimensional distributions over the different axes.
But, OK, what's the data type?
Is it a tensor?
Is it a 32-bit tensor?
Is it a uint8?
What is it?
What's the shape?
The shape of the tensors in deep learning are super critical.
Does it require gradients?
So in your problem sets, you're constantly training these networks.
And any parameter that you want to train needs to have requires gradient equals true so that you're actually getting gradients for that parameter.
What is the min?
What is the max?
What is the mean?
What is the variance?
You could go on from here, but these are the ones I like.
There are some libraries that just kind of give you this by default. But I find those sometimes change or have to require an install, or it's just a little bit-- I just like the snippet of code.
That snippet of code will work, I think, for at least a few years.
OK, so really simple, but I actually think this kind of stuff is important.
OK, so data.
Another thing is, again, the numerical range matters a lot.
So one of the standard and most useful ways of removing dependence on exactly the units in which you're measuring your inputs and your data in general is to normalize it somehow.
This is like the standardization transformation, where I take my data and I subtract the mean and divide by the square root of the variance.
This is a really common first step to any kind of data loading that you're going to do.
You load your data.
You subtract the mean, divide by the variance.
And the point that this achieves is that it makes it so that you're kind of invariant to exactly the unit of measure in which the data is stored.
So if I'm modeling some geospatial information, it doesn't matter if I've measured my data with meters or centimeters or inches or feet.
If you standardize, then it will remove the dependence on the scale of those measurements to some degree.
At least, it, makes it unit variance and zero mean.
You could also squash and squish in other ways to massage your data into a more canonical distribution.
Yeah, question?
I was going to ask, is this necessarily better than just a min, maximum-- Yeah, exactly.
So is this better than just divide by the difference between the min and the max or subtract the min divided by the difference between min and max?
Not necessarily.
Basically, you want to remove information about maybe the unit of measure, like the scale of it, or the mean of it, or possibly other statistics of it.
And there's a lot of ways of doing that.
So I'd say this is one of the most common, is just standardization.

And the other most common is probably subtract the min so that the numbers are all positive now and then divide by the max after subtracting the min so now the highest value is 1, and the lowest value is 0.
That's another very nice trick.
Now your data lies in the range 0 to 1.
OK.
And this kind of removes inductive bias about the unit of measurement, which might be good or might be bad.
So it says that no one dimension is treated as more important a priori than another dimension.
They're all in on the same scale.
They all range from 0 to 1.
Can anybody think of a case where this would be bad, where, actually, you would want to use that information about the scale?
OK, yeah?
So if you have, say, like a horizontal and vertical distance, if they are actually two-dimensional phenomenons, you wouldn't want to scale them differently.
Yeah.

If you have horizontal and vertical distance, you might not want to scale these differently because maybe distance in the vertical dimension is physically different in meaning than distance in the horizontal dimension.
Is that what you're getting at?
If they're physically the same, you'd want to scale them together as opposed to independently.
Oh.
Yeah.
So if they're physically the same, then it could be that the horizontal data has a very narrow distribution.
But you wouldn't want to therefore scale it up because now it's like you're measuring space in the horizontal axis differently than the vertical axis.
Yeah.
So there's a lot of interesting considerations that can come up where this could go wrong.
But I would say, in general, it's a good heuristic, especially when you have measurements on vastly different scales.
Like, you have some measurements that are 10 million times bigger than other measurements.

It'll be very hard for your network to learn to pay attention to the tiny measurements if there's another measurement that's 10 million times bigger, because the gradients will just be much, much smaller for the data on a smaller scale.
OK.
This slide is going to be a little more subtle.
So beware of low dimensions.
This is a slightly different thing than maybe what you've heard before.
Maybe you've taken some statistics class or even high-dimensional statistics and people said, oh, high dimensions are weird.
Beware of high dimensions.
Things are different than your intuitions in high dimensions.
OK, that's true.
So the human intuitions we have are mostly for low-dimensional, three-dimensional spaces.
The world is, like, three spatial coordinates.
Time is another dimension.
We're used to thinking in low-dimensional spaces.
We think of objects like a sphere in a low-dimensional space.
We know what that looks like.
But you may know from other classes that a sphere in high-dimensional space has slightly different properties.
So a Gaussian distribution in high-dimensional space is like a soap bubble, where almost all of the probability is in a tiny little band around the surface of the sphere.
OK.
So things are a little bit different in high-dimensional space than we're used to.
But what I want to point out is that if we weren't human and we're just some ideal creatures of math, then high dimensions is a simple one.
Things are simple in high dimensions, and they're weird in low dimensions.
And deep learning is all about getting used to thinking in high dimensions.
And everything gets simple in high dimensions.
So that's what's really nice about it.
So here's an example of that.
So we talked about RMS-norm.
Remember, Jeremy introduced that in one of his lectures.
And we sometimes will want to take the RMS norm of the activations to achieve good effects on learning dynamics.
And we also talked about layernorm, which is the standard layer in transformers, which is almost the same.
And in high dimensions, these things behave almost identically.
So the only difference is, layernorm, you subtract the mean over your vector, and then you take the RMS-norm of that vector.
In RMS-norm, you don't subtract the mean of the vector.
So RMS-norm will tend to map data points onto the unit hypersphere.
That's the effect of that operation.
So here's a visualization of the inputs.
It's like a cloud of data points.
And then the outputs, after an RMS-norm layer, are going to map everything to this unit sphere.
So that is this normalization.
You get everything onto the unit.
Well, layernorm, you might think, OK, yeah, it's basically the same operation.
And it is in high dimensions.
But in low dimensions, it has this effect.
So for 2D inputs-- this is a layernorm applied to 2D inputs.
The data points are the red points.
But layernorm is doing is by subtracting the mean-- like, the vector x is two-dimensional for a 2D space.
And we're subtracting the mean of a two-dimensional vector.
I'm losing one degree of freedom.
And now that kind of degenerates into all of my outputs have to be on-- I lost one degree of freedom, essentially.
And then the RMS norm kind of loses another degree of freedom.
So now the outputs have 0 degrees of freedom, and they end up being on these just two points as opposed to being on a one-dimensional manifold, the circle for RMS-norm.
OK.
So the point is just be careful in low dimensions.
Try to work in high dimensions as much as possible, where things are nice and simple.
And get an intuition for high dimensions.
And especially, normalization layers, like batch norm, won't work well if your batch size is small.
layernorm won't work well if your layer dimensionality is small.
Or it will have weird effects, like this.
So you have to be really careful.
I remember I had a bug-- so the work that was the most popular that I've ever been involved in was this project called Pix2Pix.
And in the initial code release of that project, I had batch norm over a batch size of 1 for one of the baselines.
And batch norm over batch size of 1 means take a data point and subtract the mean over a batch of 1.
It just take the data, subtract it.
It's 0.
So that baseline was trivially beaten.
And I corrected it.
We still beat the baseline in the end.
But that was out there for a while.
And that was just a bug.
So you can't take batch norm over batch size 1.
You can't do layernorm over layer size 1 if the dimensionality layer is 1.
OK.
So the general trick is just you're going to be working with data tensors of batch size N by M by C, maybe some other dimensions as well, these tensors.
The weights are going to be matrices N by M.
Just make sure all of your dimensions are big, and you'll be in good shape.
Yeah?
When you say big, what sort of scale do you mean?
Oh, yeah.
When I say big, what kind of scale do I mean?
Yeah, these are just heuristics.
So I don't know.
Let's say at least 10 and above, and ideally, probably as big as-- the bigger, the better, in general, I would say.
Asymptotically, everything becomes nice and simple.
Deep learning is kind of like thermodynamics.
It's really hard to say anything about a set of three or four molecules.
The three-body problem in physics is really hard to solve.
But it's very easy to say what the temperature is of a billion atoms because, asymptotically, things become very simple.
We leverage the law of large numbers.
So it's the same thing.
You always want to be toward the asymptotic limit.
OK.
What is the cost?
Well, money, time, energy.
So there is a trade-off.
There's not zero cost to increasing the scale of these things.
But for statistics and inference and prediction, bigger is better.
Yeah.
These are basically things that I've already said.
But you want to know the range of your data.
You want to know the shape of your data.

And one little trick-- this is coming from Evan-- is that if you want to sanity check your neural net architecture, don't test it on tensors in which different dimensions of the tensor all are the same number, because it makes it much harder to catch errors with reshaping.
Because it could be that you do some reshaping operations and you still get a tensor of dimension 64 in the second dimension of that tensor.
But the first dimension also should be 64.
And you actually have permuted the tensor in the wrong way, but you can't tell.
So you get kind of a better type checking to make sure the numbers all work if you use a unique set of numbers, a unique dimensionality for each dimension of the tensor.
OK.
So it's a good way of just getting syntax errors in your code.
And they'll throw a shape mismatch error when you've used unique numbers if you're getting them in the wrong order.
But they won't if you have the same dimensionality.
OK.
And yeah, be very careful with changing the types of your tensors.
If you cast a tensor as a uint8 because you think I'll save memory, well, uint8's can't represent negative numbers.
So now all your negative data, if you have negative data, will go away.
So that's the point here.
What is negative 1 for a byte?
A byte is like a uint8.
And what if I've taken my input data-- I'm like, oh, I know my input data is positive, but now I standardized it to make it lie between the unit variance and centered on 0.
So that means it can have negative values.
But I still have the intuition, well, I'm working with only positive data.
But I've standardized it.
Well, now it has negative values, but it's uint8's, and it can't have negative values.
OK, there's going to be a bug.
OK.
So you've probably gotten the feeling for this in the Psets already, but a lot of your code is just going to be reshape operations.
And this becomes a bookkeeping nightmare.
You're going to have a lot of bugs that come up just because you didn't reshape things in the right way.
You're constantly transposing, permuting, reshaping, flattening, unflattening, unsqueezing, squeezing.
This is like half the code in PyTorch.
And I personally can never remember the conventions for these things.
So if I do reshape a tensor-- let's say it's a two-dimensional tensor.
And I reshape it into a flattened array-- so just a vector of the product of the two dimensions-- is this going to stack the rows into a sequence or stack the columns into a sequence?
I don't even remember.
I don't know what this does.
Who knows, actually.
Is it going to be row major order or column major order?
If I have a matrix, is it going to read off the first row and then the next row and put it after the first row?
Does anyone know for reshape in PyTorch?
Yeah?
It's row contiguous.
OK, it's row contiguous So it does the first row, and then it takes the next one and puts it after it.
Right.
But it's hard to remember these things.
And you really don't want to have to remember all that stuff.
So this is a library that I think makes some of that a lot easier, makes keeping track of the reshape operations a little bit easier, is einops.
It doesn't mean you don't have to think at all.
And you can still have bugs with einops.
But I found it to be very helpful.
So all of the kind of reshape, flatten, unsqueeze operations now have a common notation.
They're just rearrange.
And you give a string, which is going to say-- it's kind of like a shorthand for telling the system what is the set of reshapes that will map from one space to another space.
So here, we have b, h, w, c, That means that, first, I have a four-dimensional tensor.
And I'm going to map that to h, b, w, c.
b, w are in parentheses.
That means I'll flatten those two into a single dimension.
So it'll be an h by b times w by c tensor.
It'll be a tensor with three dimensions.
And yeah, you still have to worry a little bit.
Is it the row major order or column major order?
But it makes a lot of this easier to think about.
And it tends to have the property that-- or maybe it always has the property that if I do the inverse operation, it will be an identity.

So if I do reshape b h w c to h b w c and then I do the inverse, where I do h parentheses b w c and then to b h w c, so I do the opposite direction-- if I do those one after the other, I'll get back where I started.
They're inverses of each other.
So that's a nice property.
OK.
Reshape might have that property too, but this makes it very easy.
OK.
So try einops.
OK.
As you can see, this lecture is just going to be throwing a whole lot of little tips and tricks to you.
And I'm hoping that some of them will stick and you can go and pull on these later.
OK, so data augmentation.
You did some data augmentation in Pset 1, so you know what data augmentation is.

Just a quick recap-- if I want to take small data and I want to make it bigger, there's simple tricks which you can do, which are apply transformations to your data, which should not fundamentally change it.
So you want to be able to apply transformations to, in this case, images that do not change the target class.
So this creates bigger data from smaller data.
And I think a lot of people have this impression that data augmentation is a little bit ugly, a little hacky.

And there's a whole community of people who say, oh, you should really replace data augmentation with what we might call geometric deep learning, where data augmentation is forcing invariance to this set of transformations, forcing invariance to mirror flips and crops and changing the lighting conditions very slightly, like just changing the intensity.
So data augmentation says all of those changes should have no effect on the label.
But geometric deep learning approaches say, no, I should design an invariant neural network architecture.
I should use a ConvNet to achieve translation equivariance and then pooling into two translation invariance.
And therefore, why do I need this cropping?
And there's all these arguments that I can actually use an architecture to enforce the invariances and equivariances and symmetries that I care about as opposed to data augmentation.
But I think that that's mostly not the right advice for a good hacker in machine learning.
I think the right advice is, data augmentation is really easy, really intuitive.
And it's architecture agnostic.
That's the power of it.
It's all on the data side.
So you don't have to design some fancy symmetry-preserving architecture graphnet that knows how molecule chirality should be properly propagated.
You don't have to do any of that.
You just say, OK, here's the setup of things I think are fine to do to my data.
And I'll feed that to any architecture.
I can send this to an MLP, and it will be invariant to these operations too.
So data augmentation, I think, is the way to go for most of the types of invariances you actually want.
It's just simpler.
And software engineering wise, it decouples these properties from the architecture design.
OK.
That might change.
Maybe in a few years, we'll have a very clean framework for geometric deep learning, and then we'll go to that.
OK.
But I love data augmentation.
I think it's one of the most important tools.
And there's another kind of data augmentation which is really cool, which is sometimes called domain randomization.
Oh.
OK, yeah.
So I'm just showing-- here's a visualization of what data augmentation is doing.
But I think that you probably have thought about this before.
But we have our training data.
I just make more data from little data by adding these other points by perturbing my input training data.

roadmap.lecture_goal: Apply practical and theoretical knowledge to design, debug, and generalize robust deep learning models.

objectives.text: You'll be able to understand how to use practical heuristics and deep data inspection to analyze model results, identify spurious correlations, and validate input integrity.
You'll be able to compare and apply various data scaling and normalization techniques, and utilize tensor manipulation tools to prepare data for stable deep learning training.
You'll be able to explain how data augmentation, randomization, and high-dimensional inputs contribute to improved model generalization and predictive power.
You'll be able to apply best practices for selecting, training, and optimizing deep learning models, including interpreting loss metrics and utilizing advanced smoothing techniques.

segments.subgoal: Understand the role of practical heuristics and hacks in deep learning progress

key_points.text: This lecture will focus on practical advice, heuristics, and hacks rather than formal theory.
Deep learning progress has historically been driven more by practical hacks and practitioners than by academic theory.
Classical generalization bounds, such as the VC dimension, are often vacuous and do not accurately predict the generalization ability of deep nets.
Many practical deep learning courses prioritize coding and making systems run, often treating the underlying math and theory as secondary.

key_terms.definition: Hacks are practical tips and methods that have historically driven progress in deep learning. These are often anecdotal insights from practitioners rather than formal mathematical theory.
To generalize means that a deep net can perform effectively on data that it has not encountered during the training process.
Generalization bounds are theoretical limits derived from classical theories that predict how well a system will perform. These bounds can be rendered vacuous when dealing with deep nets.

segments.subgoal: Apply the principle of deep data inspection to analyze model results

key_points.text: Researchers must look at the raw data and results, rather than just relying on summary statistics or plots.
A guiding principle is to 'become friends with every pixel' or data point in your domain.
For final projects, students should show the data itself, which should be more high dimensional than a single plot.

segments.subgoal: Identify and explain the dangers of spurious correlations in deep learning

key_points.text: High accuracy in a deep net does not guarantee that it is classifying the data for the correct reason.
A model can fail by relying on a spurious correlation or shortcut, such as looking at irrelevant features outside the target tissue.
Spurious correlations often arise from data bias, where the data itself gives away the answer.
Models that rely on spurious correlations will not generalize to new environments or datasets.

key_terms.definition: Spurious correlation is a shortcut where a deep net uses an irrelevant feature, such as a marker in the corner of an image, instead of the actual tissue to make a classification.
Bias in the data occurs when the training data itself contains a systematic skew, such as only including malignant tumors from a specific hospital, which gives away the answer.
Generalize is the ability of a model to perform accurately on new, unseen data from different contexts, such as other hospitals.
Imbalanced data set is a common failure scenario where the training data contains significantly more examples of one class than another, such as having 99% of cases being non-cancerous.

segments.subgoal: Understand why monitoring model outputs is crucial for debugging deep learning systems

key_points.text: Relying solely on the loss curve is superficial and does not provide a complete understanding of a model's training process.
For generative models, observing the model's outputs provides a higher-dimensional understanding of the training process than the loss function.
Model failures, such as plateauing performance, may be caused by physical issues or input problems rather than just optimization failure.
Effective debugging requires visualizing both the model's inputs and its outputs.

segments.subgoal: Apply data inspection techniques to validate input distributions and preprocessing steps

key_points.text: Imbalanced target outputs in training data can lead to trivial results, where the model simply guesses the majority class.
When inspecting data, it is crucial to check the range, variability of units, and whether negative numbers are possible.
A common bug occurs when the assumed data format (e.g., 0 to 1) does not match the actual loaded format (e.g., 0 to 255 uint8).
Data inspection should be performed immediately before the model's forward pass to ensure the data format matches expectations.

key_terms.definition: An imbalanced set of target outputs occurs when the training data contains a disproportionate number of one class compared to others. This imbalance can lead to trivial performance metrics if the model simply guesses the majority class.

Data preprocessing is the necessary step of preparing raw data into the specific format required for the model to process it correctly. Failure to preprocess data can lead to significant bugs, such as incorrect range assumptions.

segments.subgoal: Understand data integrity issues and inspect tensor properties in deep learning

key_points.text: Data loading errors can occur due to library conventions, such as image flipping or channel permutation (e.g., BGR vs RGB).
A mismatch between the model's expectations and the input data format causes problems during training or inference.
Critical data properties to inspect include the data type, tensor shape, and whether the tensor requires gradients.
Statistical properties like the minimum, maximum, mean, and variance are important checks for data quality.

key_terms.definition: Requires gradient is a property that must be set to true for any parameter that needs to be trained, allowing the network to calculate gradients during training.
Shape is the dimensional structure of tensors in deep learning, and this structure is considered super critical for the proper functioning of the network.
Data type specifies the format of the data, such as whether it is a 32-bit tensor or a uint8, which is an important characteristic to inspect.

segments.subgoal: Compare and contrast data standardization and min-max scaling techniques

key_points.text: Standardization involves subtracting the mean and dividing by the square root of the variance of the data.
Standardization makes the data invariant to the specific unit of measure used.
Min-Max scaling transforms data to lie within the range of 0 to 1.
Scaling is a good heuristic, especially for vastly different scales, to ensure gradients are not too small for smaller measurements.

key_terms.definition: Standardization transformation is a data normalization technique where the data is transformed by subtracting the mean and dividing by the square root of the variance. This process aims to remove dependence on the unit of measure and the scale of the data, resulting in a zero mean and unit variance distribution.

segments.subgoal: Compare how normalization techniques behave in high versus low dimensions

key_points.text: In high dimensions, things are simple, while in low dimensions, they are weird.
In high dimensions, normalization methods like RMS-norm and LayerNorm behave almost identically.
RMS-norm tends to map data points onto the unit hypersphere.
In low dimensions, the difference between normalization methods can cause a loss of degrees of freedom and data collapse.

key_terms.definition: RMS-norm is an operation that takes the Root Mean Square norm of activations, which tends to map data points onto the unit hypersphere. This operation is sometimes used to achieve good effects on learning dynamics.

Layernorm (Layer Normalization) is a standard layer used in transformers that normalizes a vector by subtracting the mean over the vector and then taking the Root Mean Square norm of the result. This operation behaves almost identically to RMS-norm in high dimensions.

High dimensions refer to spaces where the properties of data, such as a Gaussian distribution, differ significantly from human intuition derived from low-dimensional spaces. Things become simple in high dimensions, which is a key concept in deep learning.

Low dimensions refer to spaces, like the three spatial coordinates we experience, where human intuition is typically applied to understand objects and data. The lecture warns students to be careful when working in low dimensions.
Unit hypersphere is the geometric shape that RMS-norm tends to map data points onto, resulting in all data being normalized to the unit scale.

segments.subgoal: Understand how large dimensions leverage asymptotic behavior and prevent normalization failures

key_points.text: Normalization layers like Batch Norm fail when the batch size is 1, and LayerNorm fails when the layer dimensionality is 1.
For robust deep learning, all dimensions (batch size N, M, C) should be kept large, with heuristics suggesting at least 10 or more.
As dimensions become large, deep learning behavior simplifies, leveraging the law of large numbers, similar to thermodynamics.
Although increasing scale incurs costs (time, money), larger dimensions are generally better for statistical inference and prediction.

key_terms.definition: Batch norm is a normalization layer that requires a sufficiently large batch size, as taking the mean over a batch of one results in a trivial value of zero. This requirement differs from layernorm, which has constraints based on layer dimensionality.

Layernorm (Layer normalization) is a normalization layer that requires sufficient layer dimensionality to function correctly. The instructor notes that it will not work well if the layer dimensionality is small.

segments.subgoal: Apply techniques to sanity check tensor shapes and prevent data loss during casting

key_points.text: Using unique dimensions for tensor inputs helps catch errors in reshaping operations.
Casting a tensor to an unsigned integer type (like uint8) can cause negative data to be lost.
Standardizing input data often results in negative values, which cannot be represented by unsigned integer types.

key_terms.definition: Uint8 is an unsigned 8-bit integer data type. Because it is unsigned, it cannot represent negative numbers, meaning any negative data will be lost or corrupted when stored in this format.
Standardization is a process where input data is transformed to be centered on zero and have a unit variance. This transformation allows the data to contain negative values.

segments.subgoal: Introduce and demonstrate the use of einops for simplifying tensor rearrangement

key_points.text: Tensor manipulation operations like reshaping and transposing can lead to complex bookkeeping and bugs in deep learning code.
The library einops simplifies tensor operations by providing a common notation called 'rearrange'.
Einops uses a string notation to specify how dimensions map from one tensor space to another.
Einops operations often possess the property that the inverse operation returns the tensor to its original state.

key_terms.definition: Einops is a library designed to simplify complex tensor manipulation by providing a common notation for operations like reshape, flatten, and unsqueeze. This library helps make keeping track of reshape operations easier for the user.

Rearrange is a function within einops that uses a string notation to specify how a set of reshapes maps a tensor from one space to another space. This string acts as a shorthand for defining the required dimensional mapping.

Row contiguous describes the order in which a tensor is read when reshaping, meaning the operation processes the first row entirely before moving to the next row. This behavior dictates how the data is sequenced when dimensions are flattened.

An inverse operation is a sequence of operations that, when performed after an initial operation, returns the system to its original state. This property allows the original tensor to be recovered after a transformation.

segments.subgoal: Justify the use of data augmentation over designing invariant neural network architectures

key_points.text: Data augmentation increases small datasets by applying transformations that do not fundamentally change the target class.
Geometric deep learning approaches aim to design an invariant neural network architecture, whereas data augmentation forces invariance through data transformations.
Data augmentation is often preferred because it is easy, intuitive, and architecture agnostic, decoupling properties from the model design.
Domain randomization is a form of data augmentation that perturbs input training data to ensure the test data is in distribution.

segments.subgoal: Explain why increasing data difficulty improves model generalization

key_points.text: The ideal loss curve shows graceful, smooth, continual progress, indicating the problem is hard enough to learn from but not so easy that it converges too quickly.
Training on problems that converge too quickly is inefficient because it wastes optimization time (flops) in the flat region.
To improve learning, one must increase the difficulty of the data using techniques like data augmentation or domain randomization.
Making the training problem harder leads to better generalization performance.

key_terms.definition: Data augmentation is a technique that adds more data points to a dataset, which makes the learning problem more difficult for the model to solve.
Domain randomization is a method where random variation is added to the training environment to increase the difficulty of the problem, allowing the model to generalize better.

Backpropagation is the main optimization task in deep learning, involving the minimization of loss with respect to the model's parameters. This process is distinct from the alternative approach of changing the data to increase the difficulty of the learning problem.
Loss curve is a visual representation of training progress that shows how the model's loss changes over time during an experiment.
Generalization is the ability of a trained model to perform well on new test environments or data that it has not seen during the training process.

segments.subgoal: Explain how data randomization improves generalization and why data is critical in practice

key_points.text: Adding randomization makes the problem harder, forcing the model to generalize better to real-world test cases, even if it takes longer to train.
High training accuracy often indicates that the problem is too easy and needs to be made harder to generalize better.
In real-world industry scenarios, changing the data is often more impactful than changing the learning algorithm.
Companies can gain leverage by collecting more data, collecting better data, or labeling data in new ways.

key_terms.definition: Domain randomization is a technique used to minimize the gap between a source domain, such as a simulation, and a target domain, such as reality. This is achieved by introducing random variations into the source domain during training.

Generalization is the ability of a model to perform well on test cases, which are the real-world cases, rather than just performing well on the training cases. Making the problem sufficiently hard is necessary to achieve better generalization.

Robustness is the quality of a model that allows it to maintain performance even when facing variations or errors in the input data. By training with randomized inputs, the model becomes robust to potential miscalibrations or errors.

segments.subgoal: Demonstrate how increasing input information simplifies prediction problems using examples

key_points.text: Prediction becomes easier the longer the input, because more information is available for the prediction.
Historically, early NLP models (N-grams) often limited the input size (N) unnecessarily.
The more information you condition on, the easier the prediction problem becomes.
To improve predictive performance in real-world scenarios, one should add diverse information to the input features (X).

key_terms.definition: N-gram model is a statistical model that represents how words co-occur with each other in a sequence. These models are used to estimate the probability of word sequences.

Joint distribution is the statistical measure that the N-gram error models, representing the probability of all elements occurring together. This distribution considers the entire sequence of words simultaneously.

Conditional distribution is the statistical measure that the current model is designed to model, specifically the probability of the last word given the preceding words. This focuses on predicting the next element based on the input history.

segments.subgoal: Explain how high-dimensional input reduces uncertainty in deep learning models

key_points.text: Standard neural networks typically model point predictions (like regression) and do not handle complex output distributions of possibilities.
A key technique is to provide enough information in the input (X) so that the probability of the output (Y) becomes deterministic, acting like a delta function.
Modern text-to-image models succeed because they use rich input (like sentences) to make the data problem almost deterministic, allowing standard neural net methods to work.
To improve models, it is recommended to make the data big (more samples) and make the input (X) a big, high-dimensional vector.

key_terms.definition: Generative models are systems designed to handle uncertainty in the output space, moving beyond the single point predictions made by standard neural nets. Modern approaches often achieve this by modeling simple distributions, such as Gaussian distributions, conditioned on a large amount of input information.
Delta function is a mathematical representation of a single point, which occurs when the probability of an output becomes completely deterministic.
Regression is a task where standard neural net training uses functions like L2 loss to take inputs and make a single point prediction of the output value.

segments.subgoal: Explain the importance of data diversity and model simplicity in machine learning

key_points.text: When the target event in data is extremely rare, simply scaling up the data is inefficient because most of the data represents the common, well-understood case.
To improve performance in rare event detection, adding context or more information into the input data is a key strategy.
The first principle of modeling is to keep models simple, as simplicity makes them easier to understand, debug, and allows for theoretical guarantees.
Simple models are often the most powerful because the simplest model that fits the data is generally the best, following Occam's razor.
Researchers should prioritize simplicity over adding complexity just to achieve a marginal increase in accuracy on benchmarks.

key_terms.definition: Data diversity and coverage is the key factor that matters when dealing with rare classes of interest. This concept suggests that the data must adequately represent all the different things that are important in the domain.

Context is additional information added into the inputs of a model to provide surrounding circumstances. By knowing the context, a model can adjust its probability of certain states, such as reducing the probability of a crash if the context is an amusement park.

Occam's razor is an intuitive argument asserting that the simplest model that fits the data will be the best model. This principle stands apart from formalizations like generalization bounds by providing a simple, non-mathematical justification for preferring simplicity.

segments.subgoal: Use practical heuristics to select useful and widely adopted deep learning models

key_points.text: For practical systems, simplicity and popularity often matter more than raw performance.
GitHub stars are a better proxy for a model's usefulness than its accuracy on a leaderboard.
Training models on diverse or out-of-domain data is a beneficial principle.
For practical purposes, it is generally advised to use pre-trained models rather than training from scratch.

key_terms.definition: Out-of-domain data is data that is not specific to the problem being solved, and using it in the training set is beneficial because it helps put as much information into the model as possible.

segments.subgoal: Explain how to reduce image colorization to classification and justify the theoretical benefits

key_points.text: Transforming a complex problem into a known, solved problem (reducibility) helps in understanding the original problem.-
Colorization can be converted into classification by quantizing the continuous color space into discrete classes.-
A ConvNet used with a sliding window operator allows for per-pixel classification across an image.-
Classification using softmax is more expressive than regression because it models a fully expressive distribution over discrete variables.-

key_terms.definition: Quantize is the process of reducing a continuous space into discrete classes. This allows continuous values, such as colors, to be represented by distinct, countable categories.

Softmax distribution is a fully expressive categorical distribution that models a probability mass function over a discrete vocabulary. This distribution is the most general way of quantifying uncertainty over a discrete variable.

One-hot vector is a representation used to label discrete classes, similar to how labels are used in standard classification problems. Each class is represented by a vector where only one element is active.

segments.subgoal: Identify best practices and common pitfalls when designing and training deep learning models

key_points.text: A basic deep learning recipe involves transforming data into one-hot vectors and using cross-entropy classification with Adam and Transformer.
Batch normalization is discouraged because it creates a strong dependency on batch size and causes performance differences between training and testing.
Layer normalization is the current standard alternative to batch normalization.
Model performance can be improved by scaling up data, increasing model size, or training the model for a longer duration.

key_terms.definition: Batch normalization is a technique that normalizes activations using the statistics derived from a specific data batch. This process introduces a strong dependency between the model's performance and the batch size.

Batch size is a cardinal hyperparameter in deep learning that dictates how many data points are processed simultaneously during training. Batch normalization introduces a strong dependency on this parameter, which can complicate model tuning.

segments.subgoal: Apply best practices for model development and interpret deep learning loss metrics

key_points.text: Scaling is a necessary condition for achieving human-like intelligence, but it is not sufficient on its own.
Model refinement should follow an 'add, remove, remove' process until the system stops working.
When optimizing models, the process should start by overfitting to a single data point before scaling up.
In binary classification, a loss of -0.69 indicates that the model is performing at chance level.
Students should use coding assistants for learning, but must always prioritize their own thinking and understanding.

key_terms.definition: Cross-entropy loss is a metric used in deep learning to evaluate model performance, often involving the average log probability of the data under the model. Because it is based on log probabilities, the resulting loss value can be negative, which requires careful interpretation.

segments.subgoal: Understand how EMA smooths training and why deep learning design requires combining techniques

key_points.text: Exponential Moving Average (EMA) smooths values by mixing new values with previous values multiplied by a decay factor.
EMA allows replacing averaging across space (batch dimension) with averaging across time (iterates) in training.
There is no single best solution in deep learning; the optimal model requires finding the right combination of techniques.
Different components in a model serve various functions, such as regularization, increasing capacity, or speeding up optimization.

key_terms.definition: Exponentially Moving Average is a technique used to smooth out values over time. This method mixes a new value with previous values, where the contribution of older values is exponentially decayed by a specific factor.
